families.title: Worth, acceptability and deservingness
families.description: Evaluations of personal value and the conditions attached to deserving respect, love or care.

families.title: Authenticity and identity
families.description: Assumptions about remaining authentic while changing views or adapting to different settings.

subfamilies.title: Identity made dependent on a fixed role

families.title: Purpose and significance
families.description: Conditions attached to the meaningfulness of life, activity and achievement.

families.title: Learning, competence and coping
families.description: Judgments about learning, performing and coping with difficult experiences.

subfamilies.title: Capacity to cope with distressing events

families.title: Choice, decision authority and self-trust
families.description: Assumptions about choosing, disagreeing and whose judgment has authority over personal decisions.

subfamilies.title: Approval as a condition of self-trust

families.title: Influence and control
families.description: Expectations about affecting outcomes and controlling other people’s actions.

subfamilies.title: Guaranteed control as a condition of action value

families.title: Change, permanence and generalization
families.description: Expectations about whether a pattern changes, a cause persists or failure extends across domains.

subfamilies.title: Effort as removal of every limit

families.title: Acceptance, approval and social evaluation
families.description: Conditions of inclusion and expectations about judgment, admiration and the social costs of standing out.

subfamilies.title: Social costs of effort, visibility and success

families.title: Availability and continuity of connection
families.description: Expectations about receiving care, being understood and retaining valued relationships.

subfamilies.title: Unprompted recognition as proof of care
Affection treated as a fixed pool

families.title: Trust and others’ intentions
families.description: Expectations about hidden conditions, deliberate harm and exploitation.

families.title: Help, closeness and autonomy
families.description: Assumptions about assistance, reciprocity, privacy and independence within relationships.

subfamilies.title: Self-reliance and capacity costs of help
Capacity for and consequences of bonding
Receiving care creates unbearable attachment risk

families.title: Threat, adversity and the wider world
families.description: Expectations about danger, personal misfortune and the world as a place for engagement.

families.title: Uncertainty, certainty and preparation
families.description: Requirements concerning knowledge and acceptable uncertainty before deciding or acting.

subfamilies.title: Uncertain action interpreted as moral irresponsibility

families.title: Resources, opportunity and security
families.description: Assumptions about competition, resource sufficiency and subjective security.

families.title: Standards, mistakes and acceptable presentation
families.description: Criteria for acceptable work or appearance and rules about mistakes and raising standards.

subfamilies.title: Perfection as an acceptability or visibility condition

families.title: Comparison and credit for achievement
families.description: Judgments about whether achievements count and whether effort or ability receives credit.

subfamilies.title: Comparison as a condition of achievement value

families.title: Effort, productivity and rest
families.description: Conditions attached to resting and judgments about effort and the legitimacy of achievement.

subfamilies.title: Permission for and identity meaning of rest
Conditions for sustaining and resuming effort

families.title: Needs, self-assertion and boundaries
families.description: Rules about attending to personal needs, giving to others, saying no and revising boundaries.

subfamilies.title: Legitimacy and meaning of personal need
Anticipated and moral consequences of refusal

families.title: Responsibility, causation and blame
families.description: Assumptions about causing problems, preventing harm and retaining responsibility.

subfamilies.title: Breadth and persistence of prevention duty
Others' distress as evidence of wrongdoing

families.title: Fairness, reciprocity and entitlement
families.description: Beliefs about fair treatment, deserving outcomes, priority, exemptions and special treatment.

families.title: Moral membership, guilt and punishment
families.description: Requirements concerning moral or social standing, wrongdoing, punishment and forgiveness.

families.title: Meaning, expression and course of emotion
families.description: Beliefs about what feelings indicate, how they may be expressed and whether they can change.

subfamilies.title: Expression and social acceptability of emotion
Value and character meaning of emotion
Emotion as evidence about external conditions
Expected adverse consequences of positive feeling
Emotional consensus as a validity condition

families.description: Rules about enduring discomfort, waiting, acting and stopping an action.

subfamilies.title: Urge intensity and loss of choice
Prior investment creates a duty to continue

families.description: Assumptions that sustained thinking, replay or self-monitoring is needed for care, preparation or prevention.

subfamilies.title: Purposes and expected effects of repeated thinking

families.title: Mental control and uncontrollability
families.description: Requirements to control thoughts and expectations about losing control of thinking.

subfamilies.title: Requirements to eliminate or control thoughts

families.title: Memory, knowledge and revisability
families.description: Judgments about cognitive reliability, information sources, expertise, evidence and revising beliefs.

families.title: Moral significance and supposed power of thoughts
families.description: Beliefs that thought content establishes character or desire, affects external events or requires mental cancellation.

subfamilies.title: Moral significance and desire attributed to thoughts
Thought as influence on external likelihood

forms.title: Judgments
forms.description: Evaluations of character, worth, quality or value.

forms.title: Interpretations
forms.description: A thought, feeling or event is given a particular meaning.

forms.title: Predictions and possibilities
forms.description: An expected, possible or hypothetical outcome.

forms.title: Rules and requirements
forms.description: What is required, prohibited or expected as a standard.

forms.title: Conditions and dependencies
forms.description: What something depends on, requires or is claimed to be enough for.

forms.title: Capability and control
forms.description: Claims about capacity, coping, influence or control.

forms.title: Reasons and causes
forms.description: An explanation, justification or claimed causal connection.

forms.title: Rights, permission and priority
forms.description: Claims about deservingness, entitlements and whose needs come first.

beliefs.statement: My worth depends on how useful I am.
beliefs.meaning: Personal worth is asserted to depend on usefulness; the form of dependence is unspecified.
variants: My value as a person depends on my usefulness.
How useful I am is something my personal worth depends on.
questions: What do you mean by worth and usefulness here?
How does one depend on the other, if at all: a threshold, a degree, or another relationship?
beliefs.context: A contribution can matter to a role without defining a person.

beliefs.statement: If I perform poorly, I become less worthy as a person.
beliefs.meaning: Performance is converted into global personal value.
variants: A bad result lowers my value as a human being.
Doing badly makes me worth less.
questions: What would the result change about you, beyond this task?
beliefs.context: Performance can affect opportunities and formal standing.

beliefs.statement: I am worthy only when other people approve of me.
beliefs.meaning: Worth is made contingent on approval.
variants: Other people must approve of me for me to be worthy as a person.
My worth as a person requires other people's approval.
questions: What does approval provide here: opportunity, connection, or a sense of worth?
beliefs.context: Approval can affect inclusion or access to resources.

beliefs.statement: Being attractive is what makes me worth loving.
beliefs.meaning: Attractiveness is linked to being worth loving; makes may express a prerequisite, sufficiency or a constitutive criterion.
variants: My attractiveness is what makes me worth loving.
What makes me worth loving is being attractive.
questions: Does worth loving mean deserving love, receiving love, or something else?
Is attractiveness necessary, enough by itself, or part of how you define being worth loving?

readings.label: Prerequisite
readings.content: Attractiveness is necessary for being worth loving.

readings.label: Sufficiency
readings.content: Attractiveness is sufficient for being worth loving.

readings.label: Constitutive criterion
readings.content: Attractiveness constitutes what makes the person worth loving.

beliefs.context: Appearance can influence dating experiences and social treatment.

beliefs.statement: There is something fundamentally unacceptable about me.
beliefs.meaning: At least one unspecified aspect of the person is evaluated as fundamentally unacceptable; a whole-person verdict is not stated by something alone.
variants: At least one thing about me is fundamentally unacceptable.
There is some aspect of me that is unacceptable at a fundamental level.
questions: Which aspect does this judgment concern?
Does it apply to that aspect, to your whole self, or in another way?

readings.label: Unacceptable aspect
readings.content: At least one aspect is judged fundamentally unacceptable.

readings.label: Whole-person verdict
readings.content: The whole person is judged fundamentally unacceptable.

beliefs.context: Specific conduct can be unacceptable within an agreement.

beliefs.statement: Finding this difficult means I lack ability.
beliefs.meaning: Experienced difficulty is interpreted as indicating a lack of relevant ability; the ability and its scope are unspecified.
variants: Finding this hard means I lack the relevant ability.
The difficulty I experience with this means I lack ability.
questions: Which ability do you mean here?
Is this about a current skill gap, being able to learn, or something broader?
open: current skill versus capacity to learn
beliefs.context: Difficulty can reveal a specific skill gap.

beliefs.statement: I should know how to do this without being taught.
beliefs.meaning: Knowing how to do the task is expected or required without being taught; neither the force of should nor the relation to instruction is settled.
variants: I should know how to do this without anyone teaching me.
Without being taught, I should know how to do this.
questions: Does should express a requirement, an expectation, or something else?
Do you mean before any teaching, or without needing teaching in order to know?

readings.label: Requirement
readings.content: The person ought to know how to do the task without being taught.

readings.label: Expectation
readings.content: The person is expected already to know how to do the task without being taught.

beliefs.context: A role may require verified prior knowledge.

beliefs.statement: I must hide what I cannot do.
beliefs.meaning: Concealment is prescribed as a response to a skill gap.
variants: I should keep my skill gaps out of view.
Others must not see the limits of my ability.
questions: What do you expect would happen if this limitation were known?
beliefs.context: Selective disclosure may protect someone in a punitive setting.

beliefs.statement: Changing my mind would make my earlier self a fraud.
beliefs.meaning: A hypothetical change of mind is linked to judging the earlier self a fraud; deliberate prior deception is not specified.
variants: If I changed my mind, that would make my earlier self a fraud.
Changing my view would make a fraud of my earlier self.
questions: What would fraud mean about your earlier self in this statement?
Does it concern what you believed then, how you presented it, or something else?
beliefs.context: A changed account may require acknowledging prior harm.

beliefs.statement: Acting differently in different settings means I am being fake.
beliefs.meaning: Role variation is interpreted as inauthenticity.
variants: If my manner changes across groups, I am not authentic.
Presenting myself differently across settings means I am not genuinely myself.
questions: Which differences involve deception, and which involve adapting to the setting?
beliefs.context: Consistency can matter where conflicting promises are involved.

beliefs.statement: I must agree with the person in charge.
beliefs.meaning: Agreement with the person in charge is required; agreement may mean internal assent or expressed agreement.
variants: I am required to agree with the person in charge.
I have to agree with whoever is in charge here.
questions: What does agree mean here: privately share the view, express agreement, or something else?
What does the person's role actually require of you?

readings.label: Internal assent
readings.content: The person is required privately to share the authority figure’s view.

readings.label: Expressed agreement
readings.content: The person is required to express agreement with the authority figure.

notEntailed: mere cooperation being identical to agreement
beliefs.context: Coordinated action may require following a decision.

beliefs.statement: Choosing for myself means I am rejecting other people.
beliefs.meaning: Choosing for oneself is linked to rejecting others, either as an interpretation of the choice or as a claimed relational effect.
variants: Making my own choice means rejecting other people.
If I choose for myself, that means I am rejecting others.
questions: What does rejecting other people mean here?
Is the choice itself being called rejection, or do you expect a separate consequence?

readings.label: Meaning of the choice
readings.content: Choosing for oneself is itself interpreted as rejecting others.

readings.label: Relational effect
readings.content: Choosing for oneself is claimed to bring about rejection of others, as a relational act or effect.

beliefs.context: A unilateral decision can affect genuine obligations.

beliefs.statement: I must match the group to belong.
beliefs.meaning: Matching a group is presented as a requirement relative to belonging; matching is not established as sufficient for inclusion.
variants: To belong to the group, I must match it.
I have to match the group in order to belong.
questions: What would matching this group involve?
Are you describing a group condition, a rule for yourself, or both?

readings.label: Goal-linked rule
readings.content: Relative to belonging, the person requires themself to match the group.

readings.label: Practical inclusion condition
readings.content: Matching the group is claimed necessary for belonging.

notEntailed: every group having the same requirement
beliefs.context: Some shared practices genuinely define membership.

beliefs.statement: If I disagree, the group will stop including me.
beliefs.meaning: Exclusion is predicted as a consequence of dissent.
variants: Dissent will cost me my place in this group.
They will exclude me if I express a different view.
questions: What has happened to people who disagreed in this group?
beliefs.context: Can be accurate in groups that explicitly punish dissent.

beliefs.statement: People I become close to will eventually leave me.
beliefs.meaning: Closeness is linked to expected eventual departure across an unresolved domain of people; generic and universal readings remain distinct.
variants: People I grow close to will eventually leave me.
Those I become close to will leave me eventually.
questions: Which people and kinds of departure does this cover?
Do you mean a recurring expectation or every possible close relationship?

readings.label: Generic expectation
readings.content: People in the relevant class of close relationships are generally expected eventually to leave.

readings.label: Universal forecast
readings.content: Every person in the relevant class of close relationships is expected eventually to leave.

beliefs.context: An unstable relationship may provide clear evidence.

beliefs.statement: A disagreement means the relationship is ending.
beliefs.meaning: Conflict is interpreted as loss of continuity.
variants: Conflict signals that our connection is breaking.
If we argue, we are on the way to separation.
questions: What happens after disagreement in this relationship?
beliefs.context: Repeated unresolved conflict may precede an actual ending.

beliefs.statement: I have to keep checking our connection to keep it secure.
beliefs.meaning: Repeated connection-checking is presented as necessary or required relative to keeping the connection secure.
variants: I have to check our connection repeatedly to keep it secure.
To keep our connection secure, I have to keep checking it.
questions: What does checking the connection involve?
Is checking a rule you feel obliged to follow, something you believe security depends on, or something else?

readings.label: Goal-linked rule
readings.content: Repeated checking is required as a rule relative to keeping the connection secure.

readings.label: Instrumental necessity
readings.content: Repeated checking is claimed necessary for the connection to remain secure.

beliefs.context: Contact can sustain a relationship over distance.

beliefs.statement: People will not respond when I need emotional support.
beliefs.meaning: People are expected not to respond when emotional support is needed; the relevant people and strength of generalization are unspecified.
variants: When I need emotional support, I expect people not to respond.
People will not respond to my need for emotional support.
questions: Whose responses does this expectation concern?
What response would count as emotional support in this situation?

readings.label: Generic expectation
readings.content: People are generally expected not to respond to the relevant emotional need.

readings.label: Universal forecast
readings.content: Every relevant person is expected not to respond to that emotional need.

notEntailed: No one ever provides any kind of help
beliefs.context: May describe the available people accurately.

beliefs.statement: Unless someone notices my need without being told, their care does not count.
beliefs.meaning: Unprompted recognition is made a criterion of care.
variants: Care is real only when the other person notices on their own.
If I have to explain what I need, the response is not genuine care.
questions: What makes a response count as genuine care for you, and what role does noticing without being told play?
beliefs.context: Attentiveness can be an important relational expectation.

beliefs.statement: An offer of help probably has a hidden price.
beliefs.meaning: A relevant offer of help is expected probably to have an undisclosed price or condition.
variants: An offer of help is likely to have an undisclosed price.
There is probably a hidden price attached to an offer of help.
questions: What hidden price or condition do you have in mind?
Does this concern a particular offer or a wider expectation?
beliefs.context: May fit a history of manipulation or coercion.

beliefs.statement: Someone who disappoints me is trying to hurt me.
beliefs.meaning: Disappointment is attributed to hostile intention.
variants: A letdown means the other person intended harm.
When they fail me, I take it as deliberate injury.
questions: What points to intention rather than another explanation?
beliefs.context: Some harmful acts are intentional.

beliefs.statement: I must stay guarded because anyone could exploit me.
beliefs.meaning: Guardedness is required and possible exploitation is given as its reason; the scope of anyone is unresolved.
variants: I have to remain guarded because anyone might exploit me.
Because anyone could take advantage of me, I must keep my guard up.
questions: What does staying guarded involve here?
Does anyone mean each person could exploit you, an unspecified person might, or something else?

readings.label: Each-person possibility
readings.content: For each relevant person, exploitation is considered possible and used to justify guardedness.

readings.label: Unspecified threat
readings.content: Exploitation by an unspecified person is considered possible and used to justify guardedness.

notEntailed: all privacy or trust being forbidden
beliefs.context: Guardedness may be appropriate in a high-risk setting.

beliefs.statement: I should solve my problems without help.
beliefs.meaning: Self-sufficiency is treated as a requirement.
variants: I should deal with my problems on my own.
I ought to manage without relying on anyone.
questions: What would accepting help mean to you in this case?
beliefs.context: Independent practice can build a specific skill.

beliefs.statement: I cannot make this decision without someone deciding for me.
beliefs.meaning: Making this decision is said to require another person deciding on the speaker's behalf; cannot may concern capability or permission.
variants: Unless someone decides for me, I cannot make this decision.
Making this decision is not something I can do without another person deciding on my behalf.
questions: Does cannot mean being unable, not permitted, or something else?
What would the other person do: advise, approve, or make the choice for you?

readings.label: Capability prerequisite
readings.content: Another person deciding on one’s behalf is claimed necessary for being able to make this decision.

readings.label: Permission prerequisite
readings.content: Another person deciding is claimed necessary for permission to make or formalize this decision.

beliefs.context: A delegated decision can be appropriate and consensual.

beliefs.statement: Receiving help means I owe agreement in return.
beliefs.meaning: Support is linked to surrender of voice.
variants: If someone supports me, I lose the right to disagree with them.
Accepting assistance obliges me to go along with their wishes.
questions: What was actually agreed when the help was offered?
beliefs.context: Some offers explicitly include conditions that need evaluation.

beliefs.statement: Being close requires us to want the same things.
beliefs.meaning: Wanting the same things is presented as necessary for closeness; neither sufficiency nor identity of every preference is supplied.
variants: For us to be close, we have to want the same things.
Wanting the same things is required for closeness between us.
questions: Which wishes need to be the same in this statement?
What would having different wishes mean for closeness?
beliefs.context: Some commitments require negotiated common aims.

beliefs.statement: A close relationship entitles each person to know everything about the other.
beliefs.meaning: A close relationship is claimed to give each partner entitlement to know everything about the other within an unresolved information domain.
variants: In a close relationship, each person is entitled to know everything about the other.
Closeness gives each partner an entitlement to know everything about the other partner.
questions: What information does everything include here?
What do you mean by entitlement: a right to ask, to receive, or something else?
notEntailed: every conceivable information item being included
beliefs.context: Specific information may be owed under a mutual agreement.

beliefs.statement: If I stop watching for danger, something bad will happen.
beliefs.meaning: Continuous vigilance is treated as a necessary prevention.
variants: If I let my vigilance drop, something harmful will happen.
Stopping my watch for danger will be followed by something bad happening.
questions: What danger requires attention here, and when would the need end?
beliefs.context: Attention can be essential during a concrete risk.

beliefs.statement: I would be unable to cope if this feared event happened.
beliefs.meaning: Inside a hypothetical feared event, the speaker claims they would be unable to cope; the event and meaning of coping remain open.
variants: If this feared event occurred, I would not be able to cope.
I would be unable to handle it if this feared event happened.
questions: What would coping with this event involve?
Which resources or circumstances are included in the claim?
beliefs.context: The demand may truly exceed available resources.

beliefs.statement: I must know the outcome before I begin.
beliefs.meaning: Knowledge of the outcome is required before beginning; knowing is not silently replaced by eliminating every uncertainty.
variants: Before I begin, I must know the outcome.
Knowing the outcome must come before I start.
questions: What would knowing the outcome mean here?
How much information does the actual task require before beginning?
notEntailed: having knowledge guaranteeing permission or action
beliefs.context: Some actions require a defined safety or consent condition.

beliefs.statement: Not knowing means I have not prepared enough.
beliefs.meaning: Residual uncertainty is interpreted as preparation failure.
variants: Uncertainty shows that my preparation is incomplete.
If I were properly prepared, I would not have unanswered questions.
questions: Which uncertainty can preparation resolve, and which may remain?
beliefs.context: An unresolved necessary fact can reveal incomplete preparation.

beliefs.statement: I must keep checking until I feel certain.
beliefs.meaning: Subjective certainty is the stopping criterion for checking.
variants: Checking should continue while doubt is present.
A remaining doubt means I need another check.
questions: What task-based evidence would count as a completed check?
beliefs.context: Additional checking may be needed after a known error.

beliefs.statement: An uncertain outcome is unacceptable even if the risk is small.
beliefs.meaning: An uncertain outcome is evaluated as unacceptable, including under a small-risk concession; no action prohibition is stated.
variants: Even if the risk is small, an uncertain outcome is unacceptable.
An outcome that remains uncertain is unacceptable even under a small-risk condition.
questions: What makes this uncertainty unacceptable in this decision?
What kind of risk and stakes does the statement concern?
notEntailed: all uncertainty in all domains being unacceptable
beliefs.context: Very high stakes can warrant rejecting small risks.

beliefs.statement: If I plan perfectly, I can prevent every bad outcome.
beliefs.meaning: Perfect planning is claimed to enable prevention of every bad outcome; joint and outcome-by-outcome readings are not interchangeable.
variants: Perfect planning would enable me to prevent every bad outcome.
If my planning is perfect, I have the ability to prevent every bad outcome.
questions: Do you mean one plan could prevent all outcomes together, or each outcome has some possible prevention?
Which outcomes and limits are included?

readings.label: Joint prevention
readings.content: Perfect planning is claimed to enable preventing all relevant bad outcomes together.

readings.label: Outcome-by-outcome prevention
readings.content: Perfect planning is claimed to enable prevention of each relevant bad outcome, without asserting simultaneous joint prevention.

notEntailed: separate preventability implying one plan prevents all
beliefs.context: Careful planning can reduce foreseeable problems.

beliefs.statement: Nothing I do will affect the outcome.
beliefs.meaning: No action within an unresolved action set is expected to affect the specified outcome; this does not assert universal incapacity.
variants: None of my actions will affect this outcome.
Anything I do will leave the outcome unaffected.
questions: Which outcome and actions does this refer to?
Is the claim about this outcome, the present situation, or a wider range?
beliefs.context: May accurately describe an externally fixed decision.

beliefs.statement: I must stay in control of how other people act.
beliefs.meaning: Responsibility for directing other agents is assumed.
variants: I am required to keep other people's actions under my control.
How other people act must remain something I control.
questions: What authority do you have, and what depends on their choices?
beliefs.context: Some roles include limited supervisory authority.

beliefs.statement: If I can imagine a harm, I am responsible for preventing it.
beliefs.meaning: Imagining a particular harm is linked to responsibility for preventing that harm; the domain of harms and meaning of responsibility remain open.
variants: Being able to imagine a harm makes me responsible for preventing that harm.
If a harm is something I can imagine, its prevention is my responsibility.
questions: What turns imagining this harm into responsibility for preventing it?
What actual role, options and limits are involved?
notEntailed: responsibility for every conceivable event without a domain
beliefs.context: Specific duties can require response to foreseeable risks.

beliefs.statement: If someone is upset after my choice, it means I acted wrongly.
beliefs.meaning: Another person’s emotional response is treated as sufficient evidence of wrongdoing.
variants: A distressed reaction to my choice shows that the choice was morally wrong.
Another person's upset proves that my decision was morally wrong.
questions: What standard or agreement would establish wrongdoing here, apart from the reaction?
beliefs.context: A choice can cause avoidable harm that merits repair.

beliefs.statement: Delegating a task does not reduce my duty to prevent every mistake.
beliefs.meaning: Delegation is claimed not to decrease the duty to prevent every mistake; equal and increased duty are both compatible with not reduced.
variants: Delegating a task does not lessen my duty to prevent every mistake.
My duty to prevent every mistake is not reduced when I delegate the task.
questions: Does the duty stay the same, increase, or simply not decrease after delegation?
Which mistakes and responsibilities are included?
beliefs.context: Some roles retain specific accountability after delegation.

beliefs.statement: The cause of this failure will remain unchanged.
beliefs.meaning: The identified cause of this failure is expected to remain unchanged over an unspecified future interval.
variants: What caused this failure will continue unchanged.
The identified cause of this failure is expected to stay unchanged.
questions: Which cause and future period do you mean?
What exactly is expected to remain unchanged?
notEntailed: all future failures having this cause
beliefs.context: A persistent constraint may need accommodation.

beliefs.statement: A failure in this area means I will fail in other areas too.
beliefs.meaning: Failure in one area is interpreted as indicating future failure in other, unspecified areas.
variants: Failing in this area means I will fail in other areas as well.
A failure here indicates that I will fail elsewhere too.
questions: Which other areas does this extend to?
What connection do you see between the initial result and those other areas?
beliefs.context: One systemic constraint can have wide effects.

beliefs.statement: Only flawless work counts as acceptable.
beliefs.meaning: An absolute performance threshold is imposed.
variants: Any error makes the work unacceptable.
The standard is no mistakes at all.
questions: Which parts require exactness, and what defines acceptable performance elsewhere?
beliefs.context: Some bounded outputs genuinely require exact compliance.

beliefs.statement: One mistake cancels the value of everything I did well.
beliefs.meaning: An error globally invalidates an output.
variants: An error wipes out the rest of my good work.
A single flaw makes the whole effort worthless.
questions: What exactly does the mistake invalidate, and what remains useful?
beliefs.context: One critical error can make an output unusable.

beliefs.statement: If I relax one standard, all my standards will collapse.
beliefs.meaning: A bounded exception is predicted to cause broad decline.
variants: Lowering one standard will cause the rest of my standards to collapse.
An exception to one of my standards will undermine all the others.
questions: What evidence connects this exception with a wider decline?
beliefs.context: Some practices do reinforce future habits.

beliefs.statement: If others notice my skill gap, they will judge me negatively.
beliefs.meaning: A social judgment is predicted from disclosed limitation.
variants: If other people see this skill gap, I expect a negative judgment from them.
Revealing this limitation will lead others to evaluate me negatively.
questions: Who would judge you, and what makes that response likely?
beliefs.context: May fit a punitive or competitive evaluation setting.

beliefs.statement: Criticism means the other person has judged my whole character.
beliefs.meaning: Criticism is taken to indicate that the other person has evaluated the speaker's whole character; the evaluation's valence is not explicit.
variants: Criticism indicates that the other person has evaluated my entire character.
Being criticized means the other person has judged who I am as a whole.
questions: What does judged mean here: evaluated negatively, evaluated more broadly, or something else?
What makes the judgment about the whole character?
open: positive versus negative versus mixed judgment
notEntailed: actual access to another person's thoughts
beliefs.context: Some criticism really is a personal attack.

beliefs.statement: I need approval before I can trust my decision.
beliefs.meaning: Approval before self-trust is required; trusting may concern felt confidence, reliance in action or formal authorization.
variants: Before I can trust my decision, I need approval.
Trusting this decision requires approval beforehand.
questions: Does trusting the decision mean feeling confident, acting on it, or having authorization?
Whose approval and what timing are required?

readings.label: Felt confidence
readings.content: Earlier approval is required before feeling able to trust this decision.

readings.label: Reliance in action
readings.content: Earlier approval is required before relying on this decision in action.

readings.label: Formal authorization
readings.content: Earlier approval is required for authorized reliance on this decision.

notEntailed: a present approval necessarily preceding an earlier decision
beliefs.context: A regulated process may require sign-off.

beliefs.statement: If someone performs better, my achievement does not count.
beliefs.meaning: Achievement is valued only through relative superiority.
variants: Another person's better result erases the value of mine.
My success matters only if no one surpasses it.
questions: What does the comparison decide, and what does it leave unchanged?
beliefs.context: Rank can determine a specific competitive outcome.

beliefs.statement: I need exceptional achievement for my life to count.
beliefs.meaning: Life significance is conditioned on exceptional attainment.
variants: An ordinary level of success would make my life insignificant.
Only outstanding accomplishment can make my life worthwhile.
questions: What does exceptional achievement provide that seems unavailable elsewhere?
beliefs.context: An ambitious aim can be freely endorsed.

beliefs.statement: I may rest only after every obligation is finished.
beliefs.meaning: Permission to rest requires prior completion of every obligation in an unresolved set; completed obligations do not alone establish permission.
variants: Rest is permitted only after every obligation has been completed.
I am allowed to rest only once all relevant obligations are finished.
questions: Which obligations are included, and can the set be completed?
Does finishing them establish permission, or are other conditions involved?
notEntailed: finishing named tasks completing every obligation
beliefs.context: A short urgent task may reasonably precede a break.

beliefs.statement: Resting means I am lazy.
beliefs.meaning: Rest is interpreted as a character failing.
variants: Taking rest shows that I am a lazy person.
When I rest, it means that I am lazy.
questions: What distinguishes necessary rest from neglect in this situation?
beliefs.context: A pattern of avoidable neglect may need review.

beliefs.statement: Other people's needs should always come before mine.
beliefs.meaning: A universal priority is assigned against oneself.
variants: My needs belong at the end of the queue.
Whenever needs conflict, I should put the other person first.
questions: Which needs conflict here, and how should their urgency be weighed?
beliefs.context: A dependent person's immediate need may appropriately take priority.

beliefs.statement: Having needs makes me a burden.
beliefs.meaning: Need is interpreted as a negative personal load.
variants: Needing anything from others makes me too much for them.
My needs themselves are an imposition.
questions: Is the concern about a particular person's capacity or about having needs at all?
beliefs.context: A specific request can exceed available resources.

beliefs.statement: I must keep giving even when I no longer have capacity.
beliefs.meaning: Continued giving is required despite an absence of capacity; the statement does not establish that capacity is currently absent.
variants: Even when I no longer have capacity, I must continue giving.
I am required to keep giving despite having no capacity left.
questions: What kind of giving and capacity does this concern?
Which actual obligations and limits apply?
notEntailed: a particular legal or caregiving duty
beliefs.context: Emergencies can warrant temporary exceptional effort.

beliefs.statement: Saying no will bring punishment or retaliation.
beliefs.meaning: Refusal is predicted to bring punishment or retaliation in an unresolved situation.
variants: If I say no, punishment or retaliation will follow.
Refusing will lead to punishment or retaliation.
questions: Who is expected to respond, and in what way?
What evidence or actual constraints are relevant in this setting?
beliefs.context: Can be accurate under coercion or unequal power.

beliefs.statement: Saying no makes me selfish.
beliefs.meaning: Refusal is given a moral evaluation.
variants: Declining a request means I am putting myself first in a bad way.
A refusal is evidence that I am selfish.
questions: What would make a refusal fair or unfair in this case?
beliefs.context: A refusal can disregard a genuine duty in a particular case.

beliefs.statement: I must justify a boundary until the other person agrees.
beliefs.meaning: Another person's agreement is required to validate a boundary.
variants: A boundary is not justified until the other person agrees with my reasons.
I must keep explaining a limit until the other person accepts it.
questions: What explanation is owed, and whose agreement is actually necessary?
beliefs.context: Some decisions require negotiation or explanation.

beliefs.statement: Treating other people fairly guarantees that they will treat me fairly.
beliefs.meaning: Fair treatment is claimed to guarantee reciprocal fair treatment; the nature and scope of the guarantee remain unresolved.
variants: Fair treatment of others guarantees fair treatment from them in return.
If I treat other people fairly, their fair treatment of me is guaranteed.
questions: Does guarantee describe what will happen, what others owe, or an actual agreement?
Which parties and standard of fairness are involved?

readings.label: Outcome assurance
readings.content: Fair treatment is claimed to ensure reciprocal fair treatment.

readings.label: Normative assurance
readings.content: Fair treatment is claimed to establish that fair treatment is owed in return.

readings.label: Contractual guarantee
readings.content: An actual agreement is claimed to guarantee reciprocal fair treatment.

open: causal versus normative or contractual guarantee
beliefs.context: May fit a reliable reciprocal relationship.

beliefs.statement: People's misfortune shows that they did something to deserve it.
beliefs.meaning: Outcome is interpreted as evidence of deservingness.
variants: Having a misfortune means that the person deserved it.
When something bad happens to someone, that is evidence that they earned the bad outcome.
questions: What evidence connects the outcome to deservingness rather than chance or conditions?
beliefs.context: Responsibility for a specific act can be supported by evidence.

beliefs.statement: I must settle every unfairness before I can move on.
beliefs.meaning: Settling every unfairness is required before moving on; moving on may concern felt ability, permission or a rule for conduct.
variants: Before I can move on, I have to settle every unfairness.
Settling every unfairness is required before I can move on.
questions: What would settling and moving on mean here?
Is this about ability, permission, an obligation, or another kind of requirement?

readings.label: Permission condition
readings.content: One may move on only after every relevant unfairness is settled.

readings.label: Coping or readiness condition
readings.content: One feels unable to move on until every relevant unfairness is settled.

readings.label: Conduct requirement
readings.content: One must continue addressing the unfairness before proceeding.

notEntailed: actual ability to resolve every unfairness
agreement on what counts as fair
beliefs.context: Some injustices call for urgent intervention.

beliefs.statement: My sense of urgency is enough to give me priority over other people's claims.
beliefs.meaning: Urgency is treated as sufficient for priority.
variants: Feeling that I need something urgently is sufficient to put my claim first.
My felt urgency alone entitles me to go ahead of other people.
questions: What makes this urgency different from other people's claims?
beliefs.context: A genuine emergency may warrant priority.

beliefs.statement: A rule should not apply to me if it frustrates me.
beliefs.meaning: Frustration is treated as a basis for exemption.
variants: My frustration with a rule is sufficient reason to be exempt from it.
If a rule frustrates me, I should not be required to follow it.
questions: Is the concern the rule's fairness, its effects, or the feeling of restriction?
beliefs.context: A rule may genuinely be inappropriate or unjust.

beliefs.statement: Showing sadness will make others see me as weak.
beliefs.meaning: A social judgment is predicted from expression.
variants: People who see my sadness will think that I am weak.
If I show sadness, others will regard me as weak.
questions: Who might respond that way, and what has informed the expectation?
beliefs.context: Some settings do stigmatize visible distress.

beliefs.statement: I must not show anger.
beliefs.meaning: Displaying anger is prohibited; an expected consequence, justification and personal significance are not stated.
variants: I am prohibited from showing anger.
I am not permitted to display anger.
questions: What does showing anger include in this statement?
What, if anything, is the reason for the rule or the consequence you expect?
beliefs.context: Expression may need careful timing under unequal power.

beliefs.statement: If I feel embarrassed, I will not be able to cope.
beliefs.meaning: Coping failure is predicted from a specific discomfort.
variants: Embarrassment would overwhelm my ability to manage.
I could not handle being embarrassed in that situation.
questions: What would not coping look like, and what support would change the demand?
beliefs.context: The setting may involve overload or insufficient support.

beliefs.statement: I must endure this even if it harms me.
beliefs.meaning: Enduring the specified experience is required even under a harm concession; ability and actual harm are separate questions.
variants: Even if this harms me, I must endure it.
I am required to bear this experience even if it causes me harm.
questions: What exactly is required to be endured, and for how long?
What actual responsibilities, harms and alternatives are involved?
notEntailed: all forms of stopping being forbidden
beliefs.context: Some difficult duties involve unavoidable short-term costs.

beliefs.statement: A strong urge means I have to act on it now.
beliefs.meaning: Intensity is interpreted as a requirement for action.
variants: I am required to act on an urge immediately whenever it is strong.
If an urge feels powerful, I have to act on it straight away.
questions: What makes acting now necessary, beyond how strong the urge feels?
beliefs.context: Some urges convey immediate physical needs.

beliefs.statement: If I wait, I will lose the only chance.
beliefs.meaning: Waiting is predicted to eliminate the only relevant chance; the opportunity and delay interval remain unspecified.
variants: Waiting will cost me the only relevant chance.
If I delay, the only chance will be lost.
questions: Which chance and deadline does this concern?
What makes it the only relevant opportunity?
notEntailed: no other routes in every context
beliefs.context: A time-limited offer or emergency can make delay costly.

beliefs.statement: Unless I punish myself, I will repeat the mistake.
beliefs.meaning: Self-punishment is assigned a preventive function.
variants: If I do not punish myself, I will make the same mistake again.
Avoiding a repeat of this mistake requires me to punish myself.
questions: What has helped you change conduct, and what does punishment add?
beliefs.context: A strong reminder may help remember a specific commitment.

beliefs.statement: Doing one bad thing makes me a bad person.
beliefs.meaning: A global personal judgment follows a particular act.
variants: A wrong action settles what kind of person I am.
One wrongdoing defines my whole character.
questions: What needs to be judged or repaired: the act, a pattern, or the whole person?
beliefs.context: An act can be seriously wrong and require consequences.

beliefs.statement: If I forgive someone, I must trust them again.
beliefs.meaning: Forgiving someone conditionally activates a claimed duty to trust them again; trust is not made a factual prerequisite for forgiveness.
variants: Forgiving someone obliges me to trust them again.
If I forgive a person, I am required to restore trust in them.
questions: What kind of trust do you believe forgiveness requires?
Who or what sets that requirement, and in which circumstances?
notEntailed: Trust necessary for forgiveness as a fact
beliefs.context: Reconciliation may be chosen with evidence and boundaries.

beliefs.statement: Worrying is necessary for me to stay prepared.
beliefs.meaning: Worry is treated as necessary for preparedness, not merely sometimes helpful.
variants: I cannot stay prepared unless I worry.
Being prepared requires me to keep worrying.
questions: What preparation does the worrying produce, and when is it enough?
beliefs.context: Thinking ahead can produce useful plans.

beliefs.statement: If I stop thinking about a problem, I will miss its solution.
beliefs.meaning: Continuous mental review is treated as necessary for solution.
variants: Keeping the problem in mind continuously is necessary for me to find its solution.
If I take a break from thinking about the problem, I will miss the solution.
questions: What do you expect a break from thinking to change about finding a solution?
beliefs.context: Sustained analysis can help a tractable problem.

beliefs.statement: If I stop worrying, it means I do not care.
beliefs.meaning: Worry is made a necessary criterion of care.
variants: If I am not worrying, I must not care.
I count as caring only while I keep worrying.
questions: How, if at all, does worrying relate to whether you care?
beliefs.context: Worry may accompany something important.

beliefs.statement: If this thought keeps returning, I will lose control of my mind.
beliefs.meaning: Continued return of a thought is predicted to result in loss of mental control; the feared loss of control is undefined.
variants: If this thought continues to recur, I will lose control of my mind.
Continued recurrence of this thought will be followed by loss of mental control.
questions: What does losing control of your mind mean in this statement?
What change do you expect if the thought keeps returning?
beliefs.context: Unusual impairment or symptoms may need direct assessment.

beliefs.statement: Once worrying starts, nothing can interrupt it.
beliefs.meaning: Worry is judged uncontrollable.
variants: A worry episode is impossible to stop or shift.
After it begins, worry is beyond any influence.
questions: Are there times or conditions in which it changes, even briefly?
beliefs.context: Some episodes can feel difficult to shift and warrant support.

beliefs.statement: I must remove unwanted thoughts before I can continue.
beliefs.meaning: Removing unwanted thoughts is required before continuation; this may be a self-imposed permission condition or a claimed capability prerequisite.
variants: Before I can continue, I must remove the unwanted thoughts.
The unwanted thoughts must be removed before I can go on.
questions: Does must mean a rule for proceeding or a belief that proceeding is impossible?
What would count as removing the thoughts?

readings.label: Permission or rule
readings.content: Unwanted thoughts must be removed as a rule before continuation.

readings.label: Capability prerequisite
readings.content: Removal of unwanted thoughts is claimed necessary for being able to continue.

beliefs.context: A task may require rest or fewer distractions.

beliefs.statement: I ought to be able to control every thought.
beliefs.meaning: Capability to control every thought is assigned ought force; a normative standard and an epistemic expectation remain distinct readings.
variants: I ought to have the ability to control every thought.
I ought to possess the capacity to control every thought.
questions: What does controlling a thought mean here?
Is this a standard you require, a prediction of ability, or something else?

readings.label: Normative capability standard
readings.content: The person is required to possess the capability to control every relevant thought.

readings.label: Epistemic ability expectation
readings.content: The person expects to have the capability to control every relevant thought.

beliefs.context: Some reflective practices involve intentional attention.

beliefs.statement: I should trust other people's judgment more than my own in every case.
beliefs.meaning: Judgment is universally subordinated to others.
variants: I should defer to another person's judgment whenever it conflicts with mine.
In every case, I ought to give another person's view priority over my own.
questions: Who has relevant information for this particular question?
beliefs.context: Others may know more about a specific domain.

beliefs.statement: I must monitor my reactions continuously to prevent mistakes.
beliefs.meaning: Continuous monitoring is made a prevention requirement.
variants: Preventing mistakes requires me to constantly watch my own reactions.
I need continuous self monitoring to keep myself from making errors.
questions: What does monitoring detect, and how often is it actually needed?
beliefs.context: Brief monitoring can reveal a useful adjustment.

beliefs.statement: I need to understand every reaction before I can move on.
beliefs.meaning: Understanding every relevant reaction is required before moving on; understanding and the kind of prerequisite remain unspecified.
variants: Before I can move on, I need to understand every reaction.
Understanding each relevant reaction is required before I can go on.
questions: Which reactions and what degree of understanding are required?
Does moving on mean acting, shifting attention, granting permission, or something else?

readings.label: Rule or permission prerequisite
readings.content: Understanding every relevant reaction is required before permission to move on.

readings.label: Capability or readiness prerequisite
readings.content: Understanding every relevant reaction is claimed necessary for being able or ready to move on.

notEntailed: an explanation for every possible mental event
inability to act without full explanation as fact
beliefs.context: Reflection may clarify a consequential pattern.

beliefs.statement: Feeling afraid proves that the situation is dangerous.
beliefs.meaning: An emotion is treated as conclusive evidence of danger.
variants: My fear is sufficient evidence of an external threat.
If I am anxious, something unsafe must be happening.
questions: What does the fear point to, and what other information is available?
beliefs.context: Fear can be a relevant signal deserving attention.

beliefs.statement: Unpleasant emotions have no useful purpose.
beliefs.meaning: Unpleasant emotions are broadly judged to have no useful purpose; generic and exceptionless readings remain distinct.
variants: Unpleasant emotions serve no useful purpose.
There is no useful purpose served by unpleasant emotions.
questions: What would count as a useful purpose here?
Does this apply to unpleasant emotions generally or to every instance without exception?

readings.label: Broad generic appraisal
readings.content: Unpleasant emotions are broadly appraised as lacking useful purpose.

readings.label: Exceptionless appraisal
readings.content: Every relevant unpleasant emotion is claimed to have no useful purpose.

beliefs.context: An emotion may be distracting in a particular task.

beliefs.statement: Once an emotion starts, nothing can influence it.
beliefs.meaning: Emotion is judged unmodifiable.
variants: Once a feeling begins, nothing can alter its course.
Neither my actions nor changes in conditions can influence an emotion once it has begun.
questions: What affects its intensity, duration or your response, if anything?
beliefs.context: Some emotions persist despite reasonable efforts.

beliefs.statement: An expert's claim should settle the question for me.
beliefs.meaning: An expert's claim is assigned question-settling force; should may express a rule for acceptance or a judgment of evidential sufficiency.
variants: A claim from an expert should settle this question for me.
An expert's assertion should resolve the question for me.
questions: Does should settle express an obligation to accept or enough evidence to conclude?
What expertise, evidence and remaining questions are relevant?

readings.label: Acceptance rule
readings.content: The expert’s claim should be accepted as settling the question.

readings.label: Evidential sufficiency
readings.content: The expert’s claim is judged sufficient evidence to settle the question.

notEntailed: an obligation to stop all inquiry
beliefs.context: Expert consensus can be a strong practical guide.

beliefs.statement: Information from other people is generally unsafe to rely on.
beliefs.meaning: Information from others is generally evaluated as unsafe to rely on; unsafe is not silently equated with false or misleading.
variants: It is generally unsafe to rely on information supplied by other people.
Information communicated by others is generally unsafe as a basis for reliance.
questions: Which sources and kinds of information does this include?
What would make relying on the information unsafe in this context?
beliefs.context: Past misinformation may justify source-specific caution.

beliefs.statement: If certainty is impossible, all explanations are equally credible.
beliefs.meaning: Lack of certainty is equated with equal evidential support.
variants: If no explanation can be certain, none can be better supported than another.
When absolute certainty is unavailable, every explanation deserves equal confidence.
questions: What evidence distinguishes these explanations even if none is certain?
beliefs.context: Some explanations are currently equally supported.

beliefs.statement: My life needs a single overarching purpose to be worthwhile.
beliefs.meaning: One overarching purpose is made necessary for the speaker's life to be worthwhile.
variants: For my life to be worthwhile, it needs one overarching purpose.
One overarching purpose is necessary for my life to be worthwhile.
questions: What would count as one overarching purpose?
Does worthwhile refer to meaning, moral value, satisfaction, or something else?
beliefs.context: A central commitment can provide direction.

beliefs.statement: Only visible or lasting impact makes an activity meaningful.
beliefs.meaning: Meaning is conditioned on visibility or permanence of effects.
variants: An activity is meaningful only if its effects are visible or lasting.
If an activity has neither a visible effect nor a lasting one, it has no meaning.
questions: What kinds of significance are you counting or leaving out?
beliefs.context: Some projects are judged appropriately by outcomes.

beliefs.statement: Because I have been this way before, I cannot change.
beliefs.meaning: Having been a certain way before is given as a reason for being unable to change the relevant pattern; permanence is not independently established.
variants: Having been this way before is why I cannot change.
I cannot change because this is how I have been before.
questions: What pattern and kind of change do you mean?
What does the past occurrence tell you about the possibility of change now?
notEntailed: The past determining every future state
no possible support or different conditions
beliefs.context: A condition may be persistent and need accommodation.

beliefs.statement: If I try hard enough, every limitation should disappear.
beliefs.meaning: Trying hard enough is linked to every limitation disappearing; should may express an expectation or a requirement.
variants: Every limitation should disappear if I try hard enough.
Once I have tried hard enough, no limitation should remain.
questions: Does should mean you expect the limits to disappear or believe they ought to?
Which limitations and what would count as enough effort?

readings.label: Expected outcome
readings.content: Trying hard enough is expected to make every relevant limitation disappear.

readings.label: Required outcome
readings.content: If the person tries hard enough, every relevant limitation ought to disappear.

beliefs.context: Effort can matter where conditions permit development.

beliefs.statement: Another person's success leaves less opportunity for me.
beliefs.meaning: Another person's success is claimed to reduce personal opportunity in an unspecified domain; a fixed resource pool is not established.
variants: Another person's success reduces the opportunity available to me.
There is less opportunity for me as a result of someone else's success.
questions: Which opportunity is reduced, and through what mechanism?
Is the relevant pool fixed, expanding, shared, or otherwise structured?
notEntailed: every person's gain causing a loss
beliefs.context: Can be accurate in a defined zero-sum allocation.

beliefs.statement: Being a good family member requires following the expected life path.
beliefs.meaning: Following an expected life path is made necessary for good family membership; the expectation and meaning of good remain open.
variants: Following the expected life path is necessary for being a good family member.
Following the expected life path is required for being a good member of the family.
questions: Whose expectation and which parts of the life path are involved?
Does good refer to moral standing, loyalty, acceptance, or something else?
beliefs.context: A tradition can supply meaningful chosen commitments.

beliefs.statement: Feeling guilty means I have done something morally wrong.
beliefs.meaning: Guilt is treated as conclusive evidence of wrongdoing.
variants: My guilt proves that I have done something morally wrong.
If I feel guilty, I must have violated a moral duty.
questions: What duty may have been violated, apart from the feeling itself?
beliefs.context: Guilt can prompt useful review and repair.

beliefs.statement: The world is fundamentally hostile.
beliefs.meaning: The wider world is evaluated as fundamentally hostile; domain and meaning of hostility are not specified.
variants: The world is fundamentally antagonistic.
Hostility fundamentally characterizes the world.
questions: What does the world refer to in this statement?
What does hostile mean across the situations you have in mind?
beliefs.context: Adverse experiences may inform this picture.

beliefs.statement: Most things in the world are not worth exploring.
beliefs.meaning: Most things in the world are judged not worth exploring; the force of most and the criterion of worth are open.
variants: Most things in the world do not merit exploration.
Exploring most things in the world is not worthwhile.
questions: What things and what kind of exploration does this cover?
Do you mean a numerical majority or a broad impression?

readings.label: Numerical most
readings.content: A majority within a specified domain is judged not worth exploring.

readings.label: Colloquial breadth
readings.content: The world is broadly appraised as offering little worth exploring, without a numerical proportion.

open: most as majority or colloquial breadth
beliefs.context: A specific activity may genuinely offer little value.

beliefs.statement: Having a disturbing thought makes me morally bad.
beliefs.meaning: Having a disturbing thought is linked to a morally bad self-evaluation; disturbing does not independently establish immoral content.
variants: The occurrence of a disturbing thought makes me morally bad.
A disturbing thought occurring makes me a morally bad person.
questions: What makes the thought disturbing in this statement?
What conclusion does its occurrence lead to about your character?
beliefs.context: Deliberately endorsed intentions may matter to moral reflection.

beliefs.statement: Thinking about a harmful event makes it more likely to happen.
beliefs.meaning: Thinking about a harmful event is claimed to increase its likelihood; a direct mental mechanism is not specified and behavioral mediation remains open.
variants: Thinking of a harmful event increases its likelihood.
The harmful event becomes more likely as a result of thinking about it.
questions: How is thinking supposed to affect the chance of the event?
Do you mean directly, through actions or attention, or in another way?

readings.label: Direct mental effect
readings.content: Thinking about the event is claimed to affect its likelihood without a behavioral pathway.

readings.label: Mediated effect
readings.content: Thinking about the event is claimed to affect its likelihood through an unspecified pathway involving behavior or other intervening conditions.

beliefs.context: Thinking can affect events through subsequent behavior.

beliefs.statement: I must cancel a bad thought with a good thought.
beliefs.meaning: A good thought is required to cancel a bad thought; what cancellation changes is unspecified.
variants: A bad thought has to be canceled with a good thought.
I am required to use a good thought to cancel a bad one.
questions: What do cancel, bad and good mean in this statement?
What would be different after the good thought, and how would you tell?
beliefs.context: A chosen attentional shift may be useful.

beliefs.statement: I rank below other people as a person.
beliefs.meaning: The speaker ranks below an unspecified group as a person; this is not converted to a task-specific ability comparison.
variants: As a person, I am ranked below other people.
My rank as a person is below that of other people.
questions: Which dimension of rank do you mean?
Who is being compared, and by whose standard?
beliefs.context: A person may accurately recognize unequal formal status or discriminatory treatment without endorsing lower human value.

beliefs.statement: It is not enough to be accepted unless people also admire me.
beliefs.meaning: Acceptance is judged insufficient unless admiration is also present; the target for which acceptance must be enough is unspecified.
variants: Acceptance is not enough unless people also admire me.
Being accepted is insufficient unless people also admire me.
questions: What would acceptance need to be enough for?
What would admiration add in the meaning of this statement?
beliefs.context: Recognition can be a real requirement in a public performance role without being necessary in every relationship.

beliefs.statement: Being a superior kind of person gives me a stronger claim to special treatment.
beliefs.meaning: Being classified as a superior person is presented as a basis for a stronger claim to special treatment; the comparison baseline is unresolved.
variants: My being a superior kind of person strengthens my claim to special treatment.
A superior-person status gives me a stronger claim to special treatment.
questions: Stronger than whose claim or than which earlier claim?
What kind of special treatment and standard of superiority do you mean?

readings.label: Comparison with other people’s claims
readings.content: Superior-person status is claimed to make one’s claim stronger than other people’s claims.

readings.label: Comparison with one’s own baseline
readings.content: Superior-person status is claimed to strengthen one’s claim relative to the same claim without that status.

beliefs.context: Specific roles can confer agreed privileges without establishing superior human worth.

beliefs.statement: Explaining my experience will not make it understandable to other people.
beliefs.meaning: Explanation is predicted not to make an experience understandable to other people; understandability is distinct from actual understanding or agreement.
variants: Explaining the experience will not make it understandable to others.
My experience will not become understandable to other people through my explanation.
questions: What would making the experience understandable involve?
Which listeners, explanations and circumstances does this concern?
beliefs.context: May reflect repeated misinterpretation, language barriers, or an unreceptive audience.

beliefs.statement: What happened to me has left my whole self beyond meaningful recovery.
beliefs.meaning: What happened is linked to the whole self being beyond meaningful recovery; recovery is not defined as restoration of every earlier condition.
variants: What I experienced has left my whole self beyond recovery that would be meaningful.
My whole self has been left beyond meaningful recovery by what happened to me.
questions: What would meaningful recovery mean to you here?
Which effects are claimed irreversible and how does that extend to the whole self?
notEntailed: recovery meaning return to a prior state
a denial of actual lasting injury
beliefs.context: Lasting effects of harm can be real and require accommodation, care, and mourning.

beliefs.statement: When something goes wrong around me, I assume I am its main cause.
beliefs.meaning: Self-causation is adopted as a default across events before their causes are distinguished.
variants: When a problem occurs around me, I assume my actions were its main cause.
I usually attribute trouble in my surroundings primarily to myself.
questions: What happened in this instance, and what identifies your contribution among the causes?
beliefs.context: A person can have a substantial causal role in a specific incident.

beliefs.statement: Anyone who becomes close to me will inevitably be harmed by that closeness.
beliefs.meaning: Every person who becomes close is predicted to be harmed by that closeness, with inevitability claimed within an unresolved domain.
variants: Every person who becomes close to me will inevitably be harmed through that closeness.
Harm through closeness to me is inevitable for anyone who becomes close.
questions: What harm is predicted from closeness itself?
Which people, circumstances and meaning of inevitable are involved?
beliefs.context: A concrete pattern of harmful conduct can require boundaries and change; that does not establish inevitability for every relationship.

beliefs.statement: I lack the capacity to form a loving bond with anyone.
beliefs.meaning: Capacity to form a loving bond with any relevant person is denied; capacity, person-domain and temporal scope remain open.
variants: Forming a loving bond with anyone is beyond my capacity.
I do not have the capacity to form a loving bond with another person.
questions: What kinds of loving bonds and people does this include?
Is the statement about present capacity, permanent capacity, or another scope?
beliefs.context: Can name a concern about experienced connection while leaving its meaning and scope open.

beliefs.statement: My misfortunes happen because I am personally marked for bad outcomes.
beliefs.meaning: Misfortune is explained using personally marked language whose literal, metaphorical or spiritual meaning remains unselected.
variants: My misfortunes occur because I am personally marked for adverse outcomes.
My being personally marked for bad outcomes explains my misfortunes.
questions: How are you using personally marked: literally, metaphorically, spiritually, or otherwise?
What connection does that description express between you and the events?

readings.label: Literal explanation
readings.content: Being personally marked is used as a literal explanation of misfortunes.

readings.label: Metaphorical account
readings.content: Being personally marked expresses a figurative account of a pattern of misfortune.

readings.label: Spiritual account
readings.content: Being personally marked has a specified spiritual meaning within an explanatory account.

open: literal versus figurative or spiritual use
beliefs.context: Can express a person's spiritual account or metaphor of repeated adversity; neither establishes a diagnosis or causal fact.

beliefs.statement: No one could genuinely love me as I am.
beliefs.meaning: The possibility of anyone genuinely loving the speaker as they are is denied; the domain and genuine-love criterion remain open.
variants: There is no one who could genuinely love me as I am.
Genuine love for me as I am is not possible from anyone.
questions: Does this concern what currently happens or what could ever be possible?
What would genuine love as you are mean in this statement?
notEntailed: No one currently loving the speaker
change being required in every respect
beliefs.context: A present absence of affection or a history of rejection can be real without establishing universal impossibility.

beliefs.statement: My life makes me a failure as a person.
beliefs.meaning: The speaker's life is used as the basis for a failure-as-a-person evaluation; the life criterion remains unspecified.
variants: My life is what makes me a failure as a person.
On the basis of my life, I count as a failure as a person.
questions: What aspects of life support the judgment in this statement?
What does failure as a person mean by the standard being used?
notEntailed: one event alone establishing the judgment
beliefs.context: Important projects or goals can fail and deserve an honest account of loss.

beliefs.statement: People will like me only if I keep them entertained.
beliefs.meaning: Entertaining others is made necessary for continued liking.
variants: To remain liked, I have to keep other people amused or interested.
Other people's liking depends on my continual ability to entertain them.
questions: Which people require entertainment, and what happens when you are quiet or ordinary company?
beliefs.context: A particular entertainment role can legitimately require holding an audience's interest.

beliefs.statement: Because I have advantages others lack, my own distress does not qualify for support.
beliefs.meaning: Relative advantage is treated as a disqualification from acknowledging distress and seeking support.
variants: Having been fortunate disqualifies me from receiving help for my difficulties.
My advantages mean I am not entitled to seek support for distress.
questions: What makes this support available or unavailable to you, and how do your advantages enter that judgment?
beliefs.context: Resources may fairly be allocated by need, and social advantage can create real responsibilities.

beliefs.statement: I do not deserve to be cared for.
beliefs.meaning: Denial of deserving care, rather than its availability or a condition on worth.
variants: I am not deserving of care.
Being cared for is something I do not deserve.
questions: What does receiving care mean to you about what you deserve?
beliefs.context: Separate deserving care from demanding unlimited attention or describing actual neglect.

beliefs.statement: I am not capable of learning new skills.
beliefs.meaning: Learning new skills is claimed beyond capability over an unresolved skill and circumstance domain.
variants: Learning new skills is beyond my capability.
I lack the capacity to acquire new skills.
questions: Which skills and circumstances does the statement cover?
What support, access and time are included in the assessment?
notEntailed: Every specific learning difficulty being global incapacity
beliefs.context: Distinguish a general verdict from a specific learning difficulty, inaccessible instruction, disability or missing support.

beliefs.statement: My preferences should carry no weight in decisions about my own life.
beliefs.meaning: Denial of legitimate voice, rather than predicted rejection or required agreement.
variants: My own preferences should not count in decisions about my life.
Decisions about my life should give my preferences no consideration.
questions: How much consideration do you think your preferences should receive?
beliefs.context: Separate blanket exclusion of personal voice from voluntarily sharing decisions and real limits on a particular decision.

beliefs.statement: I am too different to belong anywhere.
beliefs.meaning: Difference is claimed to rule out belonging anywhere within an unresolved domain; actual exclusion and difference are not evaluated by the catalogue.
variants: My differences make belonging anywhere impossible for me.
I cannot belong anywhere because I am too different.
questions: Which differences and settings are included?
Does anywhere mean all possible groups, all available settings, or something else?
beliefs.context: Do not convert real exclusion in a particular setting, discrimination or minority identity into an internal defect. Excluded P0020 remains excluded.

beliefs.statement: No one will ever provide practical help when I am in difficulty.
beliefs.meaning: Generalized absence of practical support or protection.
variants: Whenever I face difficulty, practical help from anyone will be unavailable.
There will never be anyone to give me practical assistance when I am struggling.
questions: What kinds of help are you referring to, and from whom?
beliefs.context: Actual absence of practical resources or a safe network may be accurate; do not replace material support with cognitive reinterpretation.

beliefs.statement: Accepting help will make me incapable of managing anything on my own.
beliefs.meaning: Accepting help is predicted to cause inability to manage anything independently; the tasks, time and scope of inability remain open.
variants: If I accept help, I will become incapable of managing anything independently.
Accepting assistance will leave me unable to manage anything on my own.
questions: What would accepting help change about your own capacities?
Does anything refer to every task, managing the whole situation, or something else?

readings.label: Task-wise loss of capacity
readings.content: Accepting help is predicted to remove capacity for any relevant independent task.

readings.label: Overall management loss
readings.content: Accepting help is predicted to remove capacity to manage the relevant situation independently overall.

notEntailed: inability in every task independently unless specified
beliefs.context: Needing ongoing assistance does not establish deterioration, loss of dignity or the truth of this general consequence.

beliefs.statement: Being close to someone means giving up the right to run my own life.
beliefs.meaning: Closeness is made incompatible with personal agency.
variants: A close connection requires surrendering my right to direct my own life.
If I become close to someone, I give up the right to make choices about my life.
questions: What choices would closeness change, and how?
beliefs.context: Respect chosen interdependence. In a coercive relationship, actual loss of freedom must be addressed as a real condition.

beliefs.statement: A possible danger is probably going to happen to me.
beliefs.meaning: Possibility is treated as evidence of high personal likelihood.
variants: If a danger is possible, it is likely to happen to me.
The fact that a bad event could happen makes it probable for me.
questions: What makes this outcome seem likely rather than simply possible?
beliefs.context: Actual exposure can make a threat likely. Do not assume the likelihood estimate is inaccurate without context.

beliefs.statement: Any unfamiliar bodily sensation means I am in immediate danger.
beliefs.meaning: Unfamiliar bodily experience is treated as sufficient evidence of catastrophe.
variants: Every bodily sensation I do not recognize signals immediate danger.
An unfamiliar sensation in my body is enough to show that I am in danger right now.
questions: Which sensations are you noticing, and what do you take them to indicate?
beliefs.context: Do not infer that current symptoms are harmless or discourage medical assessment. The candidate concerns the stated blanket inference, not a diagnosis.

beliefs.statement: If I cannot guarantee the outcome, taking action is pointless.
beliefs.meaning: Partial influence is denied value without full control.
variants: Action has no point unless I can ensure the result.
Without a guaranteed outcome, doing anything is pointless.
questions: What would taking action need to accomplish to count as worthwhile?
beliefs.context: Some actions really are futile or too costly; distinguish that appraisal from a universal guarantee requirement.

beliefs.statement: Not preventing harm makes me just as blameworthy as deliberately causing it.
beliefs.meaning: Omission is morally equated with deliberate commission.
variants: Failing to stop harm makes me as blameworthy as intentionally producing it.
I bear the same blame for not preventing harm as for causing it on purpose.
questions: What responsibility do you assign to not preventing this, and on what basis?
beliefs.context: Real duties to protect exist. Clarify capacity, knowledge, role and avoidability instead of assuming an omission is blameless.

beliefs.statement: When I succeed, it is luck; my own efforts or abilities do not count.
beliefs.meaning: Success is attributed to luck and personal efforts or abilities are discounted; do not count may deny causal contribution or deny credit.
variants: Whenever I succeed, it is luck; my own efforts or abilities do not count.
My successes are luck; my own efforts or abilities do not count.
questions: Does not count mean no contribution to the result, no credit due, or something else?
What role is luck claimed to have alongside other contributors?

readings.label: Causal contribution denied
readings.content: Luck is credited as a cause and personal effort or ability is denied causal contribution.

readings.label: Credit denied
